title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM SOLOMON'S MANY WIVES
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM SOLOMON'S MANY WIVES
Some of the most dangerous things in life do not arrive looking like rebellion.
They arrive looking like blessings.
They arrive wrapped in opportunity, affection, admiration, success, influence, beauty, achievement, and everything we once prayed for.
That is the lesson that struck me when I looked deeper into the life of Solomon.
Not the young Solomon standing before God asking for wisdom.
Not the Solomon whose wisdom astonished kings and queens.
Not the Solomon who built the Temple.
Not the Solomon whose wealth became legendary.
The older Solomon.
The compromised Solomon.
The Solomon who slowly drifted.
The Solomon who teaches us one of the most terrifying truths in all of Scripture:
A person can be incredibly blessed by God and still slowly wander away from Him.
The story begins with one of the most beautiful moments in biblical history.
When God appeared to Solomon and said:
"Ask what I shall give thee." (1 Kings 3:5)
Instead of asking for riches, military power, fame, or long life, Solomon asked for wisdom.
The Hebrew word used is חָכְמָה (chokmah).
This word means far more than intelligence.
It means skill in living.
Godly discernment.
Practical wisdom.
The ability to see life from God's perspective.
God was pleased.
Very pleased.
So pleased that He gave Solomon wisdom unlike anyone before or after him.
Scripture says:
"There was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee." (1 Kings 3:12)
Imagine that.
The wisest man who ever lived.
Yet years later, that same man would become a warning to every generation.
Why?
Because wisdom without continual obedience eventually becomes knowledge without transformation.
The tragedy of Solomon was not that he lacked wisdom.
The tragedy was that he stopped submitting his wisdom to God.
The slow drift began with something that probably looked harmless.
Relationships.
Marriage alliances.
Political connections.
Strategic partnerships.
The kind of decisions that powerful leaders make every day.
Then Scripture records something shocking.
"King Solomon loved many strange women..." (1 Kings 11:1)
The Hebrew text uses the word נָכְרִיּוֹת (nokriyyot), meaning foreign women from nations God specifically warned Israel not to join themselves to spiritually.
God's concern was never ethnicity.
God created every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.
The issue was worship.
The issue was allegiance.
The issue was spiritual influence.
God knew what Solomon refused to believe:
The people closest to you will eventually shape the direction of your heart.
Scripture continues:
"He had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart." (1 Kings 11:3)
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not say they first turned away his intellect.
It does not say they first turned away his theology.
It says they turned away his heart.
Because the greatest spiritual battles are rarely intellectual.
They are affectional.
The Hebrew word for heart is לֵב (lev).
It refers to the center of desire, will, affection, thought, and devotion.
Long before Solomon's behavior changed, his heart changed.
Long before his worship changed, his loves changed.
Long before his actions changed, his affections changed.
And that is still how compromise works today.
Nobody wakes up one morning intending to abandon God.
Drift happens one affection at a time.
One compromise at a time.
One rationalization at a time.
One tolerated sin at a time.
One neglected prayer at a time.
One ignored conviction at a time.
Until one day we find ourselves standing somewhere we never intended to be.
That is why Solomon's story feels so personal.
Because many of us know what it feels like to slowly drift.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
We still attend church.
We still know the verses.
We still know the songs.
We still know the language.
But something inside feels distant.
The fire is weaker.
The hunger is smaller.
The intimacy feels interrupted.
Solomon's story reminds us that proximity to God is not the same thing as surrender to God.
Then comes one of the saddest verses in Scripture.
"For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods." (1 Kings 11:4)
The phrase "other gods" reveals the ultimate issue.
Idolatry.
The Hebrew word for worship often carries the idea of bowing down.
Giving ultimate allegiance.
Making something else the center.
Most modern idols do not look like ancient statues.
They look like careers.
Approval.
Success.
Comfort.
Relationships.
Money.
Status.
Influence.
Control.
Anything that occupies the throne reserved for Christ.
The lesson Solomon taught me is painfully simple:
Whatever captures your heart eventually directs your worship.
And whatever directs your worship eventually determines your destiny.
Yet Solomon's story is not merely a warning.
It is also a signpost pointing toward Someone greater.
Because when we turn the pages of Scripture, we meet another King.
Unlike Solomon, this King never compromised.
Unlike Solomon, this King never drifted.
Unlike Solomon, this King remained perfectly faithful.
His name is Jesus.
Where Solomon multiplied wives, Jesus pursues one Bride.
The Church.
Where Solomon's heart was divided, Jesus loved the Father perfectly.
Where Solomon's kingdom fractured, Jesus establishes an eternal kingdom.
Where Solomon failed, Christ prevailed.
This is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
The Bible is not ultimately the story of faithful people finding God.
It is the story of a faithful Savior pursuing unfaithful people.
The Greek word often translated "grace" is χάρις (charis).
It means undeserved favor.
Unearned kindness.
Divine generosity given to those who cannot earn it.
That means Solomon's warning is not the end of the story.
Neither is yours.
Maybe while reading this, you realized your heart has drifted.
Maybe your love for Christ has cooled.
Maybe compromise has become comfortable.
Maybe secret sins have become familiar.
Maybe your relationship with God feels distant.
The Gospel declares that Jesus still calls wanderers home.
Peter drifted.
David drifted.
The prodigal son drifted.
Yet grace met them.
Not because sin was small.
But because Christ is greater.
This is the heartbeat of our message:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites failures.
He rewrites regrets.
He rewrites shame.
He rewrites broken stories.
He rewrites compromised chapters.
He rewrites wandering hearts.
He rewrites people.
The lesson I learned from Solomon's many wives is not merely that compromise destroys.
It is that only Christ can keep a heart fully alive.
Wisdom alone cannot save us.
Knowledge alone cannot sustain us.
Discipline alone cannot preserve us.
We need Jesus every day.
Not merely as Savior.
But as Lord.
As King.
As the One worthy of our deepest affection.
And perhaps that is the question Solomon leaves every generation with:
What has your heart been slowly learning to love more than God?
Be honest.
This question reaches deeper than most people expect.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
You may never know how God uses a single share to redirect a wandering soul back toward Christ.
The heart rarely falls away all at once—it drifts one love at a time, until it remembers the One who loved it first.
